Class Flow

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.menukit.core.AbstractPanelElement<Flow>
com.trevlar.menukit.core.Flow
All Implemented Interfaces:
PanelElement
public final class Flow extends AbstractPanelElement<Flow>
The general reactive flow-wrap primitive — a PanelElement that holds a run of child elements and FLOWS the visible ones left-to-right into the panel's available content width, WRAPPING to new rows that grow downward when the run exceeds that width. The element analogue of SlotFlowElement (which does the same for slots, on a uniform 18px pitch); Flow handles heterogeneous, variable-width children — buttons, badges, icons, labels.

Why this exists — comprehensive wrapping

Reactive wrapping already covers text (TextLabel wraps to its budget), a button's label, and slots (SlotFlowElement). The one shape it did NOT cover was a horizontal RUN of elements wrapping to multiple rows: Row is a BUILD-TIME helper (it bakes positions once at build() and does not exist at runtime, so it can't reflow when the width changes). Flow is the runtime container that closes that gap, so wrapping is comprehensive across every content kind.

Reactive sizing — same contract as SlotFlowElement

naturalWidth() reports the ALL-children single-row width (visibility- independent), so the owning Panel's min(naturalWidth, ceiling) resolves to the screen-edge ceiling whenever the run is wider than the room available — a budget that's stable across child reveals. The flow wraps the VISIBLE children into that budget and getWidth()/getHeight() report the HUG of the wrapped layout (so the panel stays as small as the content, never reserving the full single-row width). Reactive to reveals and to a window resize, no empty space, no flash.

Owns its children's positions (§0047)

The children live INSIDE this element, not in the panel's element list — so the panel's reflow never sees them; the flow positions them itself each layout pass via setChildPosition into panel-content coordinates (flow.childX + cellX, flow.childY + cellY). Because the children then share the panel-content coordinate space the flow lives in, render is a plain child.render(ctx) and input forwarding hit-tests each child against the same content origin — no offset bookkeeping. Position is pure presentation; a child's identity is untouched.

First-class interactive host

Like ScrollContainer, Flow forwards the full input + lifecycle surface to its children (click, scroll, release, key, attach/detach, overlay), so a wrapping toolbar of Buttons behaves exactly as the same buttons would directly on the panel. A child whose interaction surface differs from its bounds (a Dropdown popover) works because the flow forwards the overlay claim. mouseClicked has no RenderContext, so the flow caches the panel-content origin from render(RenderContext)/hitTest(double, double, int, int) (the ScrollContainer idiom) to locate children at click time.

    • layoutWithin

      public void layoutWithin(int budget)
      Stores the panel's content-width budget as the wrap ceiling. Because naturalWidth() reports the (larger) all-children single-row width, the panel's min(naturalWidth, ceiling) hands us the screen-edge ceiling — stable across child reveals (it depends on screen geometry, not which children are visible).
      Parameters:
      budget - horizontal pixels available to this element, in panel content space. Always >= 1.

    • naturalWidth

    • render

      public void render(RenderContext ctx)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Renders this element. Called during the panel background pass (screen space), after slot backgrounds.

      Position the element using the context's content origin plus this element's childX/childY:

int sy = ctx.originY() + getChildY();

    • renderOverlay

      public void renderOverlay(RenderContext ctx)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Phase 18s follow-up — second-pass render hook for ELEMENTS that draw transient overlays extending outside their layout bounds (Dropdown popovers, future tooltip-like floats, expand-on-click editors). Called by the dispatcher AFTER every element's PanelElement.render(RenderContext) has run, so overlays always paint on top regardless of element declaration order.

      Default: no-op. Most elements render entirely inside their layout bounds and don't need this. Override when an element has a draws-outside-bounds region that must win z-order against sibling elements (e.g., an open Dropdown's popover that should obscure a later-declared button below it).

      Sibling to PanelElement.getActiveOverlayBounds() — that method is the INPUT-side primitive for exclusive overlay claim; this is the RENDER-side primitive for the same conceptual overlay. An element with an active overlay typically implements both: getActiveOverlayBounds returns the overlay's bounds (input claim), renderOverlay paints it. Together they make overlays inert-on-top regardless of consumer element ordering.

      Parameters:
      ctx - per-frame render context, same instance passed to PanelElement.render(RenderContext) on the base pass

    • hitTest

      public boolean hitTest(double mouseX, double mouseY, int contentX, int contentY)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Phase 14d-5 — interaction-bounds hit test. Called by the screen dispatchers (MKScreen, MKCHandledScreen, ScreenPanelAdapter) before PanelElement.mouseClicked(double, double, int) and PanelElement.mouseScrolled(double, double, double, double) to decide whether this element should receive the input event.

      Default implementation tests against the element's layout bounds — exactly equivalent to the inline screen-space bounds-check the dispatchers performed pre-14d-5. Existing elements (Button, TextField, Slider, ScrollContainer, etc.) inherit unchanged.

      Override for elements whose interaction surface differs from their layout bounds. Phase 14d-5's Dropdown is the canonical case: its popover renders OUTSIDE the trigger's layout bounds when open, and clicks on the popover area need to reach the Dropdown so it can route them internally (select-or-dismiss). Other future cases: tooltips with embedded action buttons, expandable inline editors, hover-with-click-targets.

      The split between layout bounds and interaction bounds is deliberate: panel auto-size logic uses getWidth / getHeight for layout, while the dispatcher uses hitTest for input routing. An element can claim a larger interaction surface (popover) without disturbing layout (which would cause panel reflow).

      Coordinate space: same as PanelElement.mouseClicked(double, double, int) — screen-space mouse coordinates. contentX / contentY are the panel content origin (panel position + padding); the element's screen-space top-left is contentX + getChildX(), contentY + getChildY(). The dispatcher passes its own pre-computed contentX/contentY so the element doesn't need to re-derive layout state.

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space mouse X
      mouseY - screen-space mouse Y
      contentX - panel content origin X (panel.x + padding)
      contentY - panel content origin Y (panel.y + padding)
      Returns:
      true if this element wants to receive the input event

    • mouseClicked

      public boolean mouseClicked(double mouseX, double mouseY, int button)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Called when the mouse is clicked on this element. The dispatcher hit-tests against the element's bounds before calling this method, so implementations know the click is within bounds.

      Returns true if this element consumed the click (preventing further dispatch to slots or vanilla). The default returns false, so render-only elements (TextLabel, Icon, ItemDisplay) don't need to override it.

      The button parameter is the mouse button: 0=left, 1=right, 2=middle. Core Button only consumes left-click; custom elements can handle any button.

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space mouse X
      mouseY - screen-space mouse Y
      button - mouse button (0=left, 1=right, 2=middle)
      Returns:
      true if consumed, false to let the click fall through

    • mouseScrolled

      public boolean mouseScrolled(double mouseX, double mouseY, double scrollX, double scrollY)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Called when the user scrolls the mouse wheel with the cursor over this element's bounds. The container hit-tests before calling — implementations know the cursor is within bounds.

      Returns true if this element consumed the scroll (preventing further dispatch). Default returns false, so non-scrollable elements (Button, TextLabel, etc.) don't need to override it.

      scrollX / scrollY are the wheel deltas — typically scrollY is non-zero (vertical wheel) and scrollX is zero (horizontal wheel, less common).

      Added in Phase 14d-2 alongside ScrollContainer, the first element that consumes scroll input. Existing elements default false and continue to work unchanged.

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space mouse X
      mouseY - screen-space mouse Y
      scrollX - horizontal wheel delta (typically 0)
      scrollY - vertical wheel delta (positive = up, negative = down)
      Returns:
      true if consumed, false to let the scroll fall through

    • mouseReleased

      public boolean mouseReleased(double mouseX, double mouseY, int button)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Called when the user releases a mouse button anywhere on the screen (not hit-tested against this element's bounds — the release fires regardless of cursor position, so drag-end detection works even when the user drags off the element). Default returns false for elements that don't track press/release state.

      Added in Phase 14d-2 alongside ScrollContainer to support scrollbar drag — drag is initiated in PanelElement.mouseClicked(double, double, int), and ends when mouseReleased fires (typically off-element since the cursor moved during drag). Existing elements default false and continue to work unchanged.

      Coordinate space: screen-space, same as PanelElement.mouseClicked(double, double, int).

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space mouse X at release
      mouseY - screen-space mouse Y at release
      button - mouse button (0=left, 1=right, 2=middle)
      Returns:
      true if consumed (rare for release events)

    • keyPressed

      public boolean keyPressed(int keyCode, int scanCode, int modifiers)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Keyboard input dispatch — completes the element input model alongside PanelElement.mouseClicked(double, double, int) / PanelElement.mouseScrolled(double, double, double, double). Called by the screen dispatchers on a key press while the element's panel is active. Unlike the mouse methods this is NOT hit-tested: keyboard events aren't localized to a cursor position, so every visible element on an active panel is offered the key until one consumes it.

      Returns true if this element consumed the keystroke (stopping further dispatch and suppressing vanilla's own handling of it). Default returns false, so non-keyboard elements (Button, TextLabel, …) are unaffected.

      keyCode / scanCode / modifiers are GLFW codes, matching vanilla's GuiEventListener.keyPressed. The canonical consumer is Dropdown — arrow keys move the highlighted option, Enter selects it, Escape dismisses the popover.

      Parameters:
      keyCode - GLFW key code
      scanCode - platform-specific scan code
      modifiers - GLFW modifier bitfield (shift/ctrl/alt)
      Returns:
      true if consumed, false to let the key fall through

    • getActiveOverlayBounds

      public int @Nullable [] getActiveOverlayBounds()
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Phase 14d-5 — active overlay bounds for exclusive-claim dispatch. Called by the screen dispatchers BEFORE PanelElement.hitTest(double, double, int, int) as the first dispatch pass: any element returning a non-null rect from this method gets exclusive ownership of clicks (and scrolls) that fall inside the returned region. The dispatcher routes the input solely to this element regardless of PanelElement.mouseClicked(double, double, int)'s return value, then short-circuits — no other element (including vanilla widgets behind) sees the click.

      This is the element-level parallel to M9's panel-level modal click-eat (Panel.tracksAsModal). The use case is the same: an element that draws a transient interactive overlay outside its layout bounds (e.g., Dropdown's popover when open) needs the overlay region to be inherently inert to anything behind it. Without this primitive, a click on a popover item would also fire whichever element's layout bounds happened to overlap the popover's screen region (e.g., a button paint-occluded by the popover but still hit-testable).

      Default returns null — no active overlay. Existing elements (Button, TextField, Slider, ScrollContainer, etc.) inherit unchanged. Override only when you need a transient region that's exclusively yours.

      Coordinate space: screen-space (same as the dispatchers read mouse positions). The returned rect is consumed as [x, y, width, height].

      When to use overlay vs hitTest:

      • Overlay — the element claims an exclusive region; the region "eats" all clicks/scrolls inside it (modal-like). Use when nothing behind the region should see the input (popovers, transient action menus).
      • hitTest — the element wants to be considered for dispatch when cursor is at a non-default position; if it doesn't consume, dispatch falls through to other elements. Use when the element extends its interactive surface but isn't claiming exclusivity (extended trigger zones).
      Returns:
      [x, y, width, height] of the active overlay region, or null if no overlay is active

    • notifyClickOutsideOverlay

      public void notifyClickOutsideOverlay(double mouseX, double mouseY)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Dismiss-side twin of PanelElement.getActiveOverlayBounds() — notifies an element with transient open state (a popover, an inline editor, a transient action menu) that a click landed somewhere NOT claimed by it, so it can close that state.

      The screen dispatchers call this on every visible element when a click was claimed by neither the active-overlay pass nor the hit-test pass — i.e. an "outside click." It is the element-level parallel to MKFocus.blurOnOutsideBounds(Screen, double, double), which already clears a focused TextField's focus on an outside click; this generalizes that "reset transient UI state on outside click" janitor to any popover-like element via one shared primitive (rather than each element hooking the dispatcher itself). Wired identically into every dispatcher (MKScreen, the vanilla-screen adapter, the MKC container screen) so an element behaves the same in every render context.

      Default is a no-op — elements with no transient open state inherit it unchanged. Dropdown / DropdownMulti override it to close their open popover.

      Coordinate space: screen-space, same as the dispatchers read mouse positions (the coordinates of the outside click).

      Parameters:
      mouseX - screen-space x of the click that fell outside all claims
      mouseY - screen-space y of the click that fell outside all claims

    • onAttach

      public void onAttach(net.minecraft.client.gui.screens.Screen screen)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Phase 14d-3 — screen-attach lifecycle hook. Called when the containing screen reaches its init() boundary. Default no-op for elements that don't need lifecycle hooks.

      Use case: elements that wrap vanilla widgets (e.g., TextField wraps EditBox) need to register the wrapped widget via screen.addRenderableWidget(...) so vanilla's screen widget pipeline routes charTyped/keyPressed to it when focused. Without onAttach, the wrapped widget never enters vanilla's input dispatch and IME / focus / tab navigation don't work.

      v1 fires once per screen lifetime (at init); does NOT fire on panel visibility changes mid-screen-life. Visibility-driven attach/detach is deferred — see DEFERRED.md 14d-3 follow-ons.

      Coordinate space note: at onAttach time the screen has been laid out (super.init() ran before MenuKit's lifecycle hooks fire), so panel bounds + leftPos/topPos are available. Elements that register vanilla widgets typically need to update widget coords per-frame in PanelElement.render(RenderContext) regardless of attach-time positions.

      Parameters:
      screen - the vanilla Screen the panel is attached to

    • onDetach

      public void onDetach(net.minecraft.client.gui.screens.Screen screen)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Phase 14d-3 — screen-detach lifecycle hook. Called when the containing screen reaches its removed() boundary. Default no-op.

      Mirrors PanelElement.onAttach(Screen): elements that registered vanilla widgets via screen.addRenderableWidget should remove them via screen.removeWidget(...) so vanilla's pipeline cleans up references.

      Parameters:
      screen - the vanilla Screen the panel was attached to
